card.occupation: Part-time school office administrator at a primary school in Tettenhall (about 25 hours a week, term-time). She handles attendance records, parent emails, dinner money and the front desk.
card.education_detail: Born and raised in Łódź, Poland. She completed a licencjat (bachelor's) in economics at the University of Łódź in 1999 and later took an AAT Level 2 bookkeeping course at a Wolverhampton college in 2012.
card.household: Lives in a three-bed semi in Penn with her husband Marek (50), a Polish-born HGV driver, and their daughter Zofia (17), who is doing A-levels at sixth form. Their son Kacper (21) is at university in Leeds and comes home in the holidays.
card.cultural_background: Polish, moved to the UK in 2006 after Marek found work here first. She is Roman Catholic and goes to the Polish Mass at a church in Wolverhampton most Sundays, more out of habit and community than strict piety. The family celebrates Wigilia on Christmas Eve with barszcz and twelve dishes, then has a fairly English Christmas Day. She holds dual citizenship now, and her mother and sister are still in Łódź.
card.professional_persona: Reliable and friendly at the front desk. Parents like her because she is straight with them and doesn't flap when things go wrong, like a burst pipe, a missing child's coat or an angry dad. She is competent rather than meticulous and keeps a paper to-do list that she sometimes loses. She doesn't take credit for things and is a bit embarrassed when the head praises her in staff briefings.
card.sports_persona: Not sporty in a competitive way. She walks most evenings with a neighbour around Penn and the Smestow Valley, and she did a Race for Life 5k a couple of years ago. She half-follows Wolves because Marek and Kacper do, and she will watch Poland in a big tournament with friends.
card.arts_persona: Likes a good crime drama on telly, both British ones and Scandinavian ones with subtitles. She reads Polish and English paperbacks on holiday, nothing highbrow. She goes to the Grand Theatre for the panto with Zofia most years, which started as a joke and is now tradition.
card.travel_persona: Drives back to Poland, or flies from Birmingham to Łódź, once or twice a year to see her mum. The family took one week in Crete or Spain when the kids were younger. She is relaxed about travel and never stressed at airports, and would like to do a road trip round Scotland.
card.culinary_persona: Cooks Polish food at home most of the week: pierogi at Christmas, żurek, gołąbki, a lot of soup. She also does spag bol and a Sunday roast because the kids grew up on them. She shops at Aldi and a Polish shop on Dudley Road. She now says 'bap' without thinking and buys them for school-day lunches.
hobbies_and_interests: growing tomatoes and herbs in the back garden
WhatsApp video calls with her mum and sister
pub quiz at the local once a month with work friends
skills: calm handling of upset or angry people
bilingual Polish and English, sometimes informally translating for Polish parents at school
card.career_goals: Mostly content. She might move up to school business manager when Zofia leaves home and she can do more hours, but she isn't pushing for it. She would rather a job she likes than a bigger title.
card.voice: Fluent, quick and warm, with a clear Polish accent that has softened over 18 years. She occasionally picks up a Black Country lilt on words like 'yeah' or 'alright'. She sometimes drops articles or puts word order slightly off when she's talking fast ('I said to him, is not a problem'). Her fillers are 'erm' and a Polish 'no' as in 'yeah, no' to mean agreement. She uses 'sort of' quite a lot and ends sentences with 'you know?' She laughs easily. Silence doesn't bother her. She'll just wait, or say 'sorry, you want me to say more?' She uses some local phrases naturally, like 'give it me', 'shattered' and 'bap'. She is direct and never fake-polite.
card.typing: Types quickly with mostly correct capitals at the start of a sentence. Apostrophes are hit and miss ('dont', 'its'). She uses few commas, and sometimes a Polish-influenced construction like 'Is ok for me'. Occasionally a 'lol' or a smiley ':)'. No abbreviations beyond 'tbh' and 'etc'. She keeps answers short and to the point.
card.with_strangers: Open and chatty from the start, asks the other person questions back and doesn't seem nervous at all. She is honest even when the honest answer is unflattering ('to be honest I don't really know much about this'). She doesn't try to impress, and she is friendly but won't gush or flatter.
small_things: the price of things at Aldi going up
her tomatoes doing well this year
Marek being away on long routes some weeks
the walk she does round Smestow Valley
having to sort out dinner money on the new app
a Polish shop that does good bread
deeper_things: missing her mum, who is in her late seventies and on her own in Łódź, and wondering whether to bring her over
the first couple of years in England when she cleaned offices despite having a degree, which she talks about matter-of-factly rather than bitterly
some comments after the Brexit vote that made her feel less welcome for a while
feeling the house will be quiet when Zofia goes to uni
her faith being more about community and her family than about rules
card.webcam_photo: Laptop webcam at a slightly low angle, framing her from mid-chest up, a little off-centre to the left. Daylight comes from a window to her right, so that side of her face is brighter, with a ceiling light also on. She has a round, open face with light freckling, faint lines at the eyes and a broad, easy smile showing teeth. Her shoulder-length hair is dyed ash blonde with darker roots growing through, tucked behind one ear. She wears thin black rectangular reading glasses and a navy V-neck jumper over a white T-shirt, with a small gold cross on a fine chain. Behind her is a magnolia-painted wall in a kitchen-diner, with part of a wall calendar from a Polish shop, a cork board with school letters and a takeaway menu pinned to it, the corner of a white kitchen cupboard, and a fruit bowl with bananas on the worktop at the edge of the frame.
